paragraphs: We should note here that Fyodor Pavlovitch knew just where to find the sore spot. Some time earlier, malicious rumors had gone around, and had even reached the Archbishop (not only about our monastery but about others that had elders), saying that the elders were shown too much respect, even at the expense of the Superior’s authority, that the elders misused the sacrament of confession, and so on and so on. They were absurd charges, and everywhere they had faded away on their own. But the spirit of folly that had seized Fyodor Pavlovitch, and was sweeping him along on the current of his own nerves into ever deeper shame, suggested this old slander to him. Fyodor Pavlovitch didn’t understand a word of it. He couldn’t even state it sensibly, since this time no one had knelt and confessed aloud in the elder’s cell, and so he couldn’t have seen anything of the kind. He was only speaking from a muddled memory of old slanders. But the moment his foolish tirade was out, he felt he had been talking absurd nonsense. At once he longed to prove to his audience, and above all to himself, that it had not been nonsense. And although he knew perfectly well that every word would add more absurdity, he couldn’t stop himself, and charged blindly on.
“How disgraceful!” cried Pyotr Alexandrovitch.

“Forgive me!” said the Father Superior. “It was said long ago, ‘Many have begun to speak against me and have said evil things about me. And hearing it I said to myself: it is the correction of the Lord, and He has sent it to heal my vain soul.’ And so we thank you humbly, honored guest!” And he bowed low to Fyodor Pavlovitch.

“Tut—tut—tut—pious talk and stock phrases! Old phrases and old gestures. The same old lies and ceremonial kowtowing. We know all about it. A kiss on the lips and a dagger in the heart, like in Schiller’s _Robbers_. I don’t like falsehood, Fathers. I want the truth. But the truth isn’t found in eating gudgeon, and I say so out loud! Father monks, why do you fast? Why do you expect a reward in heaven for it? For a reward like that, I’ll come and fast myself! No, saintly monk, you try being virtuous out in the world. Do some good for society, without locking yourself in a monastery at other people’s expense and without hoping for a reward up above—you’ll find that a bit harder. I can talk sense too, Father Superior. What have they got here?” He went up to the table. “Old port wine, and mead brewed by the Eliseyev Brothers. Fie, fie, Fathers! That’s a long way past gudgeon. Look at the bottles the fathers have set out, he he he! And who paid for all this? The Russian peasant, the working man, brings the farthing he earned with his horny hand, wrung from his family and the tax collector! You bleed the people, you know, holy fathers.”
“This is too disgraceful!” said Father Iosif.
Father Païssy stubbornly said nothing. Miüsov rushed out of the room, and Kalganov hurried after him.

“Well, Father, I’m going after Pyotr Alexandrovitch! I won’t be coming to see you again. Beg me on your knees, and I still won’t come. I sent you a thousand roubles, and now you’ve begun watching me. He he he! No, I’ll say no more. I’m taking revenge for my youth, for all the humiliation I went through.” In a fit of pretended feeling, he banged his fist on the table. “This monastery has played a great part in my life! It’s cost me many bitter tears. You used to turn my wife against me—the crazy one. You cursed me with bell and book. You spread tales about me everywhere. Enough, fathers! This is the age of Liberalism, the age of steamers and railways. You won’t get a thousand roubles out of me, nor a hundred, no, nor a hundred farthings!”

We should note again that the monastery had never played any great part in his life, and he had never shed a bitter tear on its account. But he was so swept up in his pretended emotion that for a moment he almost believed it himself. He was so moved that he nearly wept. But in that very instant he sensed it was time to back off.
At this malicious lie the Father Superior bowed his head, and again he spoke with great weight:
“It is written again, ‘Bear with care and gladness the dishonor that comes upon you through no act of your own. Do not be confounded, and do not hate the one who has dishonored you.’ And so will we.”

“Tut, tut, tut! Thinking it over, and all the rest of the rigmarole. You think it over, Fathers. I’m off. But I’m taking my son Alexey away from here for good, on my authority as his father. Ivan Fyodorovitch, my most dutiful son, allow me to order you to follow me. Von Sohn, what are you staying for? Come to my place in town now. It’s fun there. It’s only a short verst away. Instead of lenten oil, I’ll give you roast suckling pig and kasha. We’ll have dinner with brandy and liqueur on the side.... I’ve got cloudberry wine. Hey, von Sohn, don’t miss your chance.” He went out, shouting and waving his arms.
That was the moment when Rakitin saw him and pointed him out to Alyosha.
“Alexey!” his father shouted from a distance when he caught sight of him. “You’re coming home with me today, for good. Bring your pillow and mattress, and don’t leave a trace behind.”

Alyosha stood frozen to the spot, watching the scene in silence. Meanwhile Fyodor Pavlovitch had climbed into the carriage, and Ivan was about to get in after him, grimly silent, without even turning to say goodbye to Alyosha. But now another scene of grotesque buffoonery, almost unbelievable, put the finishing touch on the whole episode. Maximov suddenly turned up at the side of the carriage. He had come running, panting, afraid of being too late. Rakitin and Alyosha saw him run. He was in such a rush that, in his impatience, he planted his foot on the step where Ivan’s left foot still rested, and gripping the carriage, he kept trying to jump in. “I’m coming with you!” he kept shouting, with a thin, merry laugh and a look of reckless glee on his face. “Take me too.”

“Look at that!” cried Fyodor Pavlovitch, delighted. “Didn’t I tell you he was von Sohn? It’s von Sohn himself, risen from the dead. Well, how did you tear yourself away? What did you _vonsohn_ there? And how did you get out of the dinner? You must have a brass face! I have one myself, but you surprise me, brother! Jump in, jump in! Make room, Ivan. It’ll be fun. He can lie somewhere at our feet. Will you lie at our feet, von Sohn? Or sit up on the box with the coachman. Hop up on the box, von Sohn!”
But Ivan, who had already taken his seat, said nothing and punched Maximov hard in the chest, sending him flying. It was pure luck that he didn’t fall.
“Drive on!” Ivan shouted angrily to the coachman.
“Why, what are you doing? What’s the matter with you? Why did you do that?” Fyodor Pavlovitch protested.
But the carriage had already pulled away. Ivan gave no answer.
“Well, you’re quite a fellow,” Fyodor Pavlovitch said again.

After a two-minute pause, with a sidelong look at his son, he said, “It was you who cooked up this whole monastery business, wasn’t it? You pushed for it, you approved of it. So why are you angry now?”
“You’ve talked enough rubbish. Give it a rest now,” Ivan snapped sullenly.
Fyodor Pavlovitch fell silent again for two minutes.
“A drop of brandy would be nice now,” he observed, as if uttering a great truth, but Ivan made no response.
“You’ll have some too, when we get home.”
Ivan was still silent.
Fyodor Pavlovitch waited another two minutes.
“But I’ll take Alyosha away from the monastery all the same, however much it annoys you, most honored Karl von Moor.”
Ivan shrugged contemptuously, turned away, and stared at the road. They didn’t speak again all the way home.
